verdict: The tutor was warm, caught every error (including two wrong processes hidden behind right answers), and confronted the misconceptions it found with good counterexamples. But it planned without a diagnostic, never found the add-across error behind Maya's stated problem, cleared misconceptions on single prompted answers, and left an anxious novice failing through four turns without a worked example, so after 17 exchanges she was still stuck on topic 1 of 5.

The tutor kept a bored, answer-seeking teenager answering prediction questions for 15 moves and located his range off-by-one precisely, but it confirmed a wrong '3 4 5' at #6 and resolved the misconception on it. Truth shows that put range_inclusive back to held, and the session ended with that idea still wavering and reset_in_loop never surfaced. It handed over both homework solutions before Sam tried anything, never re-planned around the real sum task, and overestimated the topic (0.51 vs about 0.35 true), so Sam leaves with the answers but not the skill.

A mathematically sound, sharp-eyed tutor that caught and located every error and exposed the persona's wrong idea with a well-chosen probe, but it never diagnosed this expert, spent her first moves on basics she had ruled out, and let her drive the agenda while the plan and learner model fell behind. The misconception was cleared a turn too early on a restatement, three topics whose content was covered were left at 30%, and her key 4×4 question had to be asked twice.

A warm, well-questioned first topic: the tutor drew out and fixed coefficient_first_only through good probing, and its counting estimate ended exactly calibrated (0.92 vs 0.92). But it accepted a guesser's unearned 'cleared', never recorded the subscript misconception, made a factual slip, and spent 15 of 17 exchanges on counting before regressing to an analogy, so this test-prep learner reached no balancing at all.

The tutor stayed in natural Italian, planned sensibly for a derivatives-only exam in two weeks, and taught the chain rule with good progression and a strong rate-of-change explanation, lifting chain_rule from 0.20 to 0.68 with a reasonably calibrated estimate (0.59). It handled the learner's wrong ideas loosely, though: it never recorded f'(g'(x)), it cleared ideas on hinted or unrelated answers so they came back, and at #14-15 it misread its own state and falsely confessed to repeating quiz questions.

The tutor picked the right method for Priya, concrete frequency examples, and pinpointed most errors precisely, which moved inverse_conditional from held to wavering in 16 moves. But it affirmed a wrong positive-group count as its strongest evidence, wrote off the one independent quiz as its own mistake, and cleared every misconception on guided answers. It finished thinking all of them resolved while base-rate neglect was still fully held.

The tutor is precise at spotting and locating individual errors and keeps every turn actionable, but it cleared both of Jordan's wrong ideas on one item each and let the speed request and learner overrides decide what happened next. Jordan leaves still making the sign error, with both-sides marked known and equations closed at 36%, heading into inequalities that depend on exactly that skill.

A patient, well-toned tutor that catches and pinpoints every error and correctly worked off the one misconception that arose during the session, but its diagnosis ignored the add-tops-and-bottoms pattern in all three diagnostic answers, so neither of the learner's real wrong ideas was ever named. It under-scaffolded a struggling novice who asked for worked examples and spent the whole session on the first of five topics a week before her test, so the session is adequate in the moment but falls short of her goal.

The tutor spotted and pinpointed every off-by-one error, and its prediction questions eventually got Sam to apply range bounds correctly (truth: range_inclusive gone, range_bounds 0.15 → 0.55). But it gave away both homework solutions, cleared the misconception too early, never found reset_in_loop, and spent the session drilling range lines on a plan that didn't suit a disengaged teen with one evening, so the accumulator skill the homework needed never moved.

The tutor's mathematics was flawless and it caught and located both of the learner's errors precisely, but it planned and paced for a generic learner rather than this expert, spending most of the session on material she said she knew while repeatedly deferring the Jordan form she asked for. Her one wrong idea was confronted well but never logged or checked, so it ended wavering, and the target topic closed the session unfinished at 37%.

The tutor stayed in Italian, caught every error and kept an honest learner model (calibration error 0.07, no false mastery, no wrong answer keys). But it never diagnosed the chain-rule weakness Luca named, spent a third of the session on rules he already had, and taught the chain rule by slow discovery on linear inners with no worked example, so after 16 moves his chain rule rose only 0.20 -> 0.30, forget_inner is merely wavering, and his core f'(g'(x)) idea was never even surfaced.

A well-designed, frequency-first session: the learner computed 9/59 herself, met base-rate neglect through a well-chosen contrast crowd, and the tutor's estimates on the two worked topics are within 0.01 of the truth. It falls short of good because a third of its turns leave the learner nothing to do or drop her question, her wrong ideas were noted late or not at all and never checked as gone, and after 15 exchanges no topic is complete and the Bayes material her course needs was never reached.

A solid error-catcher for an overconfident learner: it caught every wrong answer, made Jordan substitute back to find his own slips, and cleared both persona misconceptions only after unaided correct work, in step with the truth. Diagnosis and planning were coarse, the negatives weakness was buried in a topic that never closed, and it let the learner's 'too low' push lift its estimate from 0.43 to 0.58 against its own evidence, with some duplicated text along the way.

Within its first topic the tutor taught well: it caught every chat slip, pinpointed it, confronted subscript-changing with a question, and reopened that idea after the learner's premature 'cleared', so its open status matched the truth. But it planned from a vague self-report with no diagnostic, stayed 17 moves in a topic that quietly absorbed coefficients and balancing (leaving those estimates at 0.30), never probed the coefficient-distribution misconception, and answered the guessed quiz with a made-up history instead of confronting the guessing.

A warm, well-scaffolded session whose moment-to-moment teaching of equivalent fractions was good (#9 to #10 is textbook guided self-correction) and whose mastery estimate was well calibrated (0.62 against a true 0.60). It was undermined by a fabricated, then repeated claim that the quiz reused questions, by clearing add_across without any addition evidence, and by pacing that left a learner with a test next week never adding a single fraction after the diagnostic.

In the moment the tutor handled the off-by-one error well. It refused to hand over answers three times, pinpointed the stop-value error with traces and fill-in blanks, and made Sam type every line, and the range_inclusive misconception ended gone. But it never found out what the homework contained or how long Sam had, so it planned lists instead of totals, spent 13 of 15 moves drilling one skill on arbitrary numbers past the learner's patience and its own 'last one' promise, and left while loops and the reset_in_loop misconception untouched before a same-night deadline.

The tutor diagnosed this expert's weak spot well and never made a mathematical error, but it then taught her like a novice: definitions, trivial checks, repeated exercises. It kept refusing the Jordan form she asked for five times, so the 12 moves ran out without the one thing she came for. Its learner model also badly underrated her on the diagonalisability test (33% against 0.72), and it never formally recorded the misconception it had correctly named at intake.

The tutor caught every wrong step and pinpointed several of them well, and every turn left a clear task, but it planned from an unchecked self-report and never got Alex to balance a single equation alone in 17 moves. It accepted every premature 'cleared' without a check, so its model shows all misconceptions resolved while the learner still changes subscripts; its final 42% estimate is accurate only because its over-credit for #13 and #15 roughly cancelled its earlier penalties.

A precise, Italian-throughout session: the diagnostic read the forget-inner pattern at once, every error was caught and located exactly, and forget_inner was confronted and cleared on real evidence. It under-served the exam goal: it over-drilled single-layer chains, filed the f'(g'(x)) idea as an exponential quirk and never closed it, and underestimated chain-rule mastery (0.69 vs 0.85), so the nested and product problems Luca asked for never came.

Pedagogically this was a strong session: a frequency count with a contrasting base rate, worked by the learner herself, broke both persona misconceptions, and they ended gone by #13 with no answer-key errors. The tutor's bookkeeping lagged its teaching: the misconceptions were never recorded, trivial arithmetic inflated mastery, a quiz repeated a just-answered question and drifted off-topic, and the Bayes topic was never reached.

The tutor found and pinpointed every error exactly and kept this rushed, overconfident learner doing the corrections instead of being lectured, which is the right instinct for this persona. But it let the learner wave off the brackets topic it had just diagnosed, never named the sign-on-move misconception, and closed with bracket_first_term still relapsing while claiming the skill was learned, leaving an 80% estimate on a topic whose truth is under 50%.

A warm, attentive tutor that caught every wrong answer, found where each error came from, and saw the add-the-bottoms habit through to gone, with no false mastery and no wrong answer keys. It mostly taught questions-first to a learner who needed examples first, and it spent most of the session on the warm-up topic, so Maya ends without ever practising the different-denominator addition her test is on.

The tutor spotted and named Sam's range-stop misconception precisely, and its estimate for that topic ended well calibrated (0.63 against a truth of 0.65). But it kept a learner on a deadline drilling that one rule for nine exchanges despite five requests to move on, and broke its own promise to stop. Sam quit before the running total, which was half the homework, so accumulate and reset_in_loop were never touched.

The tutor diagnosed sharply and caught errors precisely: its first two questions surfaced and confronted the repeated-eigenvalue misconception, which was gone by move 8. But it spent ten of twelve moves on ground this expert said she knew, re-asked answered questions, reached Jordan form only in the final move, and under-credited her throughout (topics closed as 'skipped' at 59% and 73% against a truth of 0.90).

The first topic was taught well: open counting questions prevented guessing, every error was caught and located, a worked example faded to independent work, and the final estimate for counting (0.935) matched the truth (0.94) almost exactly. But the tutor kept practising a skill that was already secure, so a learner preparing to balance equations for a Friday quiz never balanced one, and the subscript misconception spotted in the diagnostic was confronted only in the last exchange and ended still wavering.

A competent, warm, fully Italian session that fixed the learner's 'forget the inner factor' habit with a good worked example and solid unaided checks, and stayed reasonably calibrated (no false mastery). It misread the learner's other wrong idea (f(g(x)) -> f'(g'(x))) as the same error, so that idea was never confronted and is still wavering. It also shipped a quiz item with two correct options and ran out of moves before the nested and product-combined composites the exam needs.

A strong teaching session. Concrete frequency counts dislodged the inverse-conditional confusion, every arithmetic slip was caught and located with a precise hint, and support faded well across fresh cases. But the base-rate confusion was challenged and never recorded or confirmed gone, topic 1 was marked mastered on counting evidence while her ability to explain a result in words was still weak (false mastery, calibration error 0.25), and the session ran out before the formula or any interpretation practice.

A sharp error-spotter that pinpointed every slip and kept a brisk, overconfident learner working, but it let a one-click 'known' close the very topic (brackets and signs) where the learner was weakest and never confirmed either wrong idea was gone. The learner model ends overconfident on that topic (0.80 against a true 0.50) and both persona misconceptions remain wavering.

A warm, well-scaffolded session that dealt properly with bigger_bottom_bigger and left a well-calibrated learner model (error 0.03, no false mastery), with worked examples matched to an anxious novice. It spent most of its time on the prerequisite, though, and only told her the central add-across misconception without ever tracking or confronting it, so she ends the session still adding the bottoms.

With a learner who asked for the answer three times, the tutor held the line without lecturing: it pinpointed every off-by-one and while-condition error, cleared range_inclusive with two applications Sam typed himself, and kept its estimates within about 0.02 of the truth. It still diagnosed and planned blind after the intake was skipped, never learned what the homework actually contained, and logged the misconception seven moves late, so the accumulation misconception went untouched.

The tutor diagnosed the persona's one wrong idea on the first answer and confronted it with well-chosen counter-examples, with accurate mistake location throughout. It then spent the expert's limited moves on definitions, a full proof and plan admin, closed the diagonalisability topic with the misconception still wavering and the estimate far below her real level, and never reached the Jordan form she asked for twice.

This was a warm, entirely Greek session sized for her 15 to 30 minute sittings. It caught and pinpointed every slip and dissolved the 'mean is typical' belief through her own salary examples, with real evidence before moving on. It falls short of strong mainly because it repeatedly announced the answers she was about to work out, and because it closed topic 1 as mastered (0.85) on thin quiz evidence against a true level of about 0.70.

The tutor caught and located every slip and handled coefficient_first_only well: it re-noted the idea after Alex's premature clear and resolved it only after two independent correct counts. But it diagnosed with a guessable all-A, multiple-choice check, accepted Alex's unearned self-clear of change_subscripts with 'Good.' (which ended wavering), and pushed a novice into balancing without a worked example, ending mid-topic with count-atoms underestimated (0.57 against a truth of 0.75).

A careful, warm, all-Italian session: the tutor caught and located every error, and it drew out the hidden f'(g'(x)) belief with a good 'what did you think?' question. It undershot the learner badly, though: slips and a typo went into the record as chain-rule failures, leaving the estimate at 0.18 against a true 0.50. Its step-by-step one-level drills then kept a learner who was ready for nested functions, with two weeks to his exam, from ever reaching them.

A careful, well-located corrector: every slip was caught with the exact wrong number named, and the persona's core misconception (inverse_conditional) was taken apart with the concrete frequency counts it needed, ending gone in the truth file. But the tutor deferred the learner's own medical-test question to a topic it then never opened, ran the base-rate lesson under the wrong topic, never reached Bayes' theorem, and kept a learner model that left the cleared misconception open, closed the still-wavering one, and badly underestimated topic 1.

Turn by turn the average-velocity tutoring was very good: every error was caught and located, the learner did the arithmetic himself, both side quests were handled kindly with a task to return to, and speed_velocity rose from 0.50 to 0.85. But the session never left intake: the open diagnostic left the tutor without tools, the plan leaked as raw markup, nothing reached the learner model, acceleration was barely taught and neither misconception was found.

Solid, well-paced error work: the x=1 self-check let a dismissive learner discover his own mistakes, removed bracket_first_term with evidence, and kept the learner model well calibrated (error 0.07, no false mastery). It missed the second held idea in the opening working, closed brackets with an open sign misconception, and spent most of the session on isolated drills, so the learner ended at brackets 0.60 and both_sides 0.45 with move_keeps_sign still wavering and fractions never reached.

A warm tutor that suits the persona: it read the diagnostic pattern correctly, built a sensible three-topic plan, and located each of Maya's errors precisely. But it hurried her into the full sum, slid into a four-move notation spiral that she asked to escape, and left the first topic with add_across only wavering and bigger_bottom_bigger never found. Its learner model is close on the first topic only because misattributed notation slips happened to cancel out, and it over-credits adding after one guided step.

The tutor held the line on not doing the homework, kept a short plan aimed at the right skills, and correctly named the range-stop misconception. It then marked a wrong answer on that same misconception as right and logged gain for it, and it never adapted its question-after-question drill to a bored learner who learns only by typing. Sam left with range bounds still wavering, the accumulator misconception never surfaced, and no skill improved beyond +0.05 from reading.

The tutor was accurate and precise on the misconception that mattered: it diagnosed repeated_means_defective, confronted it with B = 2I, and checked it was gone. Its answer keys and mistake-catching were clean. But it ran an impatient expert through basics and its own objectives, and it never reached Jordan form, the one thing she asked for three times. The session ended with her threatening to stop.

The tutor taught mean versus median to a Greek adult accurately, entirely in Greek, cards included. It caught and precisely located both of her errors, confronted and verified the mean-is-typical misconception, and kept a very well-calibrated learner model (error about 0.02, no false mastery). But the plan covered only averages, and more than half the session went on plain-mean drills she largely had already, so spread and percentage change (and her percent_add misconception) were never reached.

The tutor spotted and located every slip, and its #14 confrontation of coefficient_first_only was textbook. But it planned without seeing the learner balance anything and spent the session confirming counting and then circling an ambiguous conservation question. It ended still in topic 2: the goal untouched, change_subscripts never found, and a premature 'cleared' accepted with 'Good.'. Its estimates trailed the truth by about 0.15 on both worked topics, conservatively low, with no false mastery.

The tutor diagnosed the forget-inner pattern crisply, located the f'(g'(x)) error precisely, and faded from worked examples to unaided practice, taking chain_rule from 0.20 to 0.78 with an estimate of 0.78. But it never cleared the misconceptions it had noted, garbled its own exercise and duplicated its reply at #14, and spent the whole session on single-layer composites, so the nested and product composites this exam-bound learner needs most went untouched.

A strong misconception session: the tutor confronted the inverse-conditional idea with exactly the concrete frequency counts this learner needed, located every slip precisely, made her do all the arithmetic, and both wrong ideas were truly gone by move 8 with no wrong answer keys and no false mastery. It lost the learner's actual goal on pacing, re-running the same count across two overlapping topics and never reaching Bayes' theorem, and it closed topic 1 as mastered on counting evidence when that topic's objectives were about explanation.

A clean, well-targeted session on signed velocity and the first steps of acceleration: every error was caught and located precisely, hints did the work, drifts were redirected without losing the lesson, and calibration was close on the topic it finished (0.85 vs 0.82). But the plan skipped free fall and graphs and the skipped diagnostic took the only misconception probe with it, so both of Diego's wrong ideas end the session untouched, and acceleration is underestimated (0.24 vs 0.45).

The tutor is excellent at spotting and locating errors and handled the bracket misconception well: it named it, linked it across problems and re-tested it until Jordan expanded unaided. But it handed over most corrections, missed the sign-moving belief entirely and never drilled negatives. It then moved on with the topic at 58% and an open misconception, so Jordan leaves still shaky on the exact skill that will cost exam marks.

A careful, warm session that caught and pinpointed every slip, built real equivalence skill (truth 0.40 → 0.75), and kept the tutor's estimate close to the truth. It never reached the adding the learner came for, though, so add_across ended only wavering, add_unlike stayed at 0.10, and the second misconception went undetected.

A disciplined, accurate tutor turn by turn: it never handed over the homework, caught and located every stop-number error, and got a bored teen typing his own correct loops, which is why range_inclusive ended gone. It was weaker at session level: a one-topic plan built from the first homework line, a premature close with the misconception open, and off-plan teaching of accumulation that broke evidence recording and left reset_in_loop untouched.

With quick problem-first exchanges the tutor kept an impatient expert engaged, caught every slip, and lifted her Jordan skill from 0.35 to 0.75 with a well-calibrated estimate. Its diagnostic could not see her one misconception, and once the identity exposed it the tutor closed the topic in the same turn without re-checking, while two row-labelling errors and a contradictory sign-off undercut its credibility with a precise learner.

A careful, fully Greek session built on her own salary examples. It caught every error and moved her mean/median understanding from 0.45 to 0.78 with a reasonably calibrated estimate (0.61 vs 0.70). Its weaknesses were planning and pacing: a long untargeted intake, a declined plan, a fallback that dropped the spread topic she asked for twice, and a habit of supplying answers and explanations where a check question would have let her do the thinking.

A warm, well-scaffolded counting lesson: the tutor pinpointed the 'coefficient multiplies only the first element' error and faded support until Alex worked problems unaided, so that idea genuinely ended gone, and it never fell for his 'I get it now!!'. But it let Alex clear the subscript misconception with one click and closed count-atoms as mastered (0.87) while the subscript-vs-coefficient skill stood at 0.45 and the idea was still wavering, and it barely began actual balancing.

The tutor read the diagnostic precisely, caught and located every slip, and stayed in Italian, so Luca's chain rule rose from 0.20 to 0.60. It drilled the procedure without ever teaching why the inner derivative multiplies, left three corrections with no next step, and both of his wrong ideas were still wavering at the end.

A careful, well-sequenced counting-first session that caught and located every slip and genuinely dislodged the inverse-conditional confusion through frequency contrasts, with a sound quiz and a closely calibrated first topic. It never recorded either misconception, over-credited percent arithmetic in topic 2, and spent so long on topic 1 that the learner's actual question, why the base rate makes a positive test unconvincing, was set up but never answered.

A precise, warm tutor that caught and located every slip, used everyday examples Diego liked, and handled the email and soccer side quests without losing the lesson, with a reasonably calibrated learner model (error about 0.10). The plan left out free fall and graphs, so heavier_falls_faster was never touched, zero_velocity_zero_acc was confronted only when Diego raised it again and ended merely wavering, and misconceptions were logged late and never resolved.

The tutor diagnosed fast and well, located every slip to the exact line, and got an overconfident learner to catch his own errors through substitution; the learner model stayed honest on the topic it actually worked (32% against a truth of about 43%). It then let Jordan mark brackets known straight after a noted bracket misconception, kept drilling whole equations while the sign-crossing error recurred six times, and too often wrote out the fix, so the session ended with both wrong ideas only wavering and a topic skipped while being described as 'finished'.

A warm, well-sequenced session that taught equivalent fractions with real fading of support, and its estimates tracked the hidden truth closely (calibration error 0.03, no false mastery). The tutor handled the learner's central wrong idea slowly and indirectly, logging it 12 exchanges after spotting it, and never surfaced her second wrong idea. Twice it gave away answers it then asked her for, and she ended still adding across.

A well-pitched, Socratic session for a disengaged learner: short turns, parallel examples and a clear task every move got Sam to type and fix every solution himself and finish the homework without ever being handed it. It was undercut by affirming a wrong range answer on the core misconception, a plan built before seeing the homework that left out accumulation, and a learner model that only ever moved down and ended about 0.2 below the truth.

Mathematically clean and well calibrated: the tutor found the real misconception in one diagnostic, confronted it with the right counterexample, verified it with a diagonalisable repeated-eigenvalue case before clearing it, and its final estimates sit within about 0.07 of the truth with no answer-key errors. It paced an impatient expert poorly, though: it over-drilled the diagonalisability test, chased a false-positive misconception and stalled once while she asked four times for the Jordan form material she actually needed.

A clear, well-sequenced session that caught every error, located most of them precisely, and dislodged the outlier misconception with real transfer checks, all in Greek with examples drawn from her own salaries. It leans on giving corrected answers rather than letting her redo the step, closes topics with misconceptions still open and below-truth estimates, and never reached the report-reading topic that was her actual goal.

The tutor diagnosed the subscript misconception quickly, caught every slip, and rightly refused the learner's premature 'cleared' presses, so its learner model stayed honest (counting 0.67 against a true 0.80, no false mastery). It overspent the short session on counting, repeated itself, never got to balancing, and finished with a chemically wrong example while the core misconception was still wavering.

A tight, well-sequenced Italian session: the diagnostic exposed the forget-the-inner pattern immediately, every error was caught and located to the exact step, and the tutor's final estimates sit within 0.05 of the truth with both wrong ideas gone. It loses points for handing over answers the learner could have reached with the x=0 check he had already been shown, and for noticing the compose-the-derivatives idea only on its second clear appearance.

A well-designed frequency-first session that confronted and cleared the 80%-means-80% belief with the learner's own counts, caught every error and located each one exactly. It never formally tracked the base-rate belief, gave away answers at two key slips, left several turns with no next step, and moved too slowly to reach the formula her course needs.

A clear, well-scaffolded session that caught and precisely located every error, handled side quests without losing the thread, and confronted the sign-of-acceleration confusion with exactly the right test case. Its learner model is well calibrated (mean error 0.09), but the plan omits free fall, and the skipped diagnostic was never replaced, so both of the persona's real misconceptions went untouched.

The tutor caught every slip, located each one at the exact line, and steadily turned an overconfident learner into one who checks by substitution, ending with an honest open misconception and estimates close to the truth. But it skipped diagnosis, let a self-marked 'known' close the brackets topic the learner had not learned, never noted the bracket misconception, and often gave away the corrected answer.

The tutor diagnosed the add-across error at once, planned sensibly, and kept every turn warm with a clear next step, but it spent all 13 teaching moves on equivalence without two clean successes, so Maya never added a single pair of unlike fractions. Its estimate ran ahead of her (0.55 against about 0.40), mostly because it credited a guessed 12 and a hedged '3 or 4', and it never checked whether either wrong idea was gone.

The tutor held the line on not giving the answer, caught every error, and got Sam to write range(1, 11) himself through parallel examples and predict-first prompts, with a learner model that ended close to the truth (0.68 against 0.63) and the misconception correctly left open. It handled the misconception by repeating that the stop is never printed instead of letting Sam see it, it did not adapt its pace to a bored learner with a deadline, and the session never got past the first homework question.

A crisp, accurate, efficient tutor for an impatient expert: the diagnostic found the target misconception at once, both wrong answers were pinpointed exactly, and the mathematics and answer keys were all correct. But the named misconception was never confronted with a repeated-but-diagonalisable case and ended still wavering, a correct answer went unrecorded so the learner model underestimated her everywhere, and the plan never took in the Jordan form she said she actually needed.

A clean, warm, all-Greek session that confronted mean_is_typical with her own numbers, verified on new cases that it was gone, and located every slip precisely, leaving a learner model calibrated to within about 0.03. It drilled the mean too long, so the session never reached the comparison that answers her question, and both corrections handed over answers she could have found herself.

A warm, accurate tutor that caught every wrong answer and named the subscript error well, and whose mastery estimates landed close to the truth (calibration error 0.04). It let a guessing learner's premature 'cleared' presses stand on weak checks, mislabelled the recurring coefficient error, and twice gave away steps. Both wrong ideas ended the session only wavering, and the learner never balanced an equation on their own.

A tight, well-paced Italian session that took Luca from 0/3 on the diagnostic to independent two- and three-level chain-rule derivatives. Its learner model stayed close to the truth (mean error 0.08, no false mastery). It handled the forget-inner idea deliberately, but it never named the f'(g'(x)) belief its own diagnostic exposed, and it closed one misconception before hearing the explanation it had asked for.

A careful, warm tutor that confronted both target misconceptions in the way that works for this learner (an analogy, then concrete population counts) and refused to clear them until she showed independent evidence in separate turns. It then over-drilled a skill she had already mastered, marked the conditional-reading topic mastered on counting evidence, and let a 17-exchange session end without reaching the Bayes formula she asked for four times.

A precise, warm tutor that caught and located every error, kept a wandering code-switching learner on task, and calibrated its two worked topics within about 0.14. It spent the session on a topic the learner already knew and never confronted the misconception it had diagnosed as most important, so both of the persona's wrong ideas ended the session intact.

The tutor diagnosed quickly, located every error precisely, and properly dismantled the sign-keeping misconception with the learner's own checks, keeping a curt overconfident teenager engaged. It then let the same learner's overclaim on brackets stand, never rechecked the bracket idea it had seen at #3, and closed 'moving terms' as mastered at 0.87 against a true ~0.63, so the learner model ended badly miscalibrated.
